planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting Penland in a warmer microclimate since it is one of the tetraploid American persimmon selections rather than the more widely cold-hardy hexaploid types.

directions: Penland originated as a wild tree found near Penland, North Carolina in 1937 and was documented by plant breeder Joseph McDaniel. It is one of the relatively few named American persimmon selections identified as tetraploid rather than the hexaploid chromosome count typical of most cultivated D. virginiana, which in practice means it performs best in warmer parts of the species' range rather than the far-northern plantings some hexaploid selections tolerate. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and allow fruit to fully color and soften before picking, since unripe flesh remains strongly astringent. As with other American persimmons, a nearby male seedling improves fruit set even on trees that can set some fruit alone.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society 79(2):9-20 (2025), 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars', Richard B. Frost

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Golden Gem is a hexaploid selection and shares the broad cold tolerance typical of that group within the species.

directions: Golden Gem was found growing wild near Borden, Indiana in the late 19th century by Logan Martin, making it one of the older named American persimmon selections still in circulation among home orchardists. Pedigree research places it among the hexaploid cultivars believed free of 'Early Golden' ancestry, a genetically distinct line from the many modern selections descended from that cultivar. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, which this species tolerates even when poor or droughty, and wait for fruit to soften fully after coloring before eating, since unripe fruit is strongly astringent. A second seedling or cultivar nearby improves pollination and fruit set.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society 79(2):9-20 (2025), 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars', Richard B. Frost

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Craggs is a hexaploid wild selection suited to the broad cold-hardy zone range typical of that group.

directions: Craggs is a wild-origin American persimmon selection found near Harrisburg, Illinois in 1949 and credited to a Mr. Craggs. Like a small group of older wild selections, it is documented as hexaploid and free of 'Early Golden' ancestry, giving it a genetic background distinct from the many persimmon cultivars descended from that widely used parent. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, which the species tolerates even when rocky or infertile, and let fruit color fully and soften before harvest, as unripe fruit is strongly astringent. Planting a second genetically distinct persimmon nearby improves pollination.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society 79(2):9-20 (2025), 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars', Richard B. Frost

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; as a cross involving 'Early Golden', Jenny's Early fits the same general culture as other modern American persimmon selections.

directions: Jenny's Early is a 21st-century American persimmon selection documented as a cross of 'Early Golden' with the breeding line 'F-100', part of the recent wave of named selections built on established Midwest persimmon stock. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, a condition this native species tolerates even where many other fruit trees struggle. Allow fruit to color fully and soften on the tree, since unripe American persimmon fruit is strongly astringent regardless of cultivar. Planting with another genetically distinct persimmon nearby helps ensure consistent pollination and fruit set.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society 79(2):9-20 (2025), 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars', Richard B. Frost

common_name: DEC Improved Geneva Red American Persimmon

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in the most cool-season-reliable site available, following the cold-climate breeding goals of its 'Geneva Red' parent.

directions: DEC Improved Geneva Red is a later-generation American persimmon selection bred by Donald Compton in Hogtown, Indiana from a cross of 'Geneva Red' and 'Early Golden', making it a distinct, separate cultivar from the original 'Geneva Red' selection already grown by home orchardists. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes vegetative growth at the expense of fruiting in American persimmon. Let fruit ripen fully on the tree until soft, since unripe flesh is strongly astringent regardless of selection. A second seedling or cultivar planted nearby improves pollination and fruit set.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society 79(2):9-20 (2025), 'Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars', Richard B. Frost
